extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and creative writers interested in mythology and storytelling
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and evaluative criteria for creating or analysing mythic narratives and the hero's-journey/story structure, including archetypes, functions of myth, cultural variation, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monomyth / Hero's Journey
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell's concept of monomyth (one myth) refers to the theory that sees all mythic narratives as variations of a single great story. The basic structure can be classified using stages such as the Call to Adventure, Receiving Supernatural Aid, Meeting with the Goddess/Atonement with the Father and Return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archetypal stages as a template for narrative progression: departure, initiation, return. Employ universal motifs and symbols to evoke the deeper, shared human pattern; examples include Krishna, Buddha, Jesus, and modern iterations such as Star Wars. Be explicit about stage functions (e.g., call, ordeal, boon) when structuring plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes and Jungian symbolic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell made heavy use of Carl Jung's theories on the structure of the human psyche and often used terms such as anima, animus and ego consciousness. His conception of myth is closely related to the Jungian method of dream interpretation, which is heavily reliant on symbolic interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In crafting characters and imagery, map recurring psychological archetypes (mentor, shadow, anima/animus) to narrative roles and symbolic motifs. Use symbols to access a reader's psyche, remembering that archetypal resonance comes from broadly shared human patterns rather than idiosyncratic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of myth — Mystical/Metaphysical
rubrics_metrics.description: Awakening and maintaining in the individual a sense of awe and gratitude before the 'mystery of being'. Mythological symbols act as 'being statements' pointing beyond literal description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes, images, or motifs that evoke awe and a sense of mystery; use ritualized or symbolic moments to give readers experiential access to transcendent themes rather than explaining them didactically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of myth — Cosmological
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining the shape of the universe. For pre-modern societies, myth functioned as a proto-science offering explanations for physical phenomena (seasons, life cycles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When worldbuilding, craft myths that account for natural patterns or cosmology in ways that illuminate cultural values and motivate rituals or behaviors within the story world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of myth — Sociological
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate and support the existing social order. Campbell contrasted 'Right Hand Path' myths that reinforce conformity with 'Left Hand Path' patterns like the Hero's Journey that demand surpassing social norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a story's mythic elements should legitimize social structures or challenge them; use myth to dramatize social tensions and the protagonist's relationship to community values (conformity vs. revolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of myth — Pedagogical/Psychological
rubrics_metrics.description: Guide the individual through the stages of life. Myth may serve as a guide for successful passage through psychological and life-stage challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure character arcs to mirror rites of passage or psychological development stages; use mythic episodes as didactic but experiential passages for growth rather than mere exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor as 'being statements' (use metaphors, not similes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Campbell, metaphors (as opposed to similes) 'pretend to a literal interpretation' and point beyond themselves into the transcendent — e.g., 'Jesus is the Son of God' rather than 'the relationship... is like that of a son to a father'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor metaphoric, literal-seeming statements and imagery that assert rather than compare, to create a stronger mythic register. Use metaphorical claims to carry spiritual or existential weight in the narrative, but balance with accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of myth — cultural stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths evolve through stages reflecting cultural development: The Way of the Animal Powers (hunting/gathering), The Way of the Seeded Earth (early agrarian), The Way of the Celestial Lights (first high civilizations), and The Way of Man (medieval/modern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor mythic motifs to the socio-economic and cosmological contexts of the culture you depict. Use appropriate symbolic priorities (animals, fertility, celestial order, romantic person-to-person themes) to give myths historical depth and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance universal patterns (elementary ideas) with cultural particulars (folk ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell distinguished 'elementary ideas' (prime matter of the monomyth) from 'folk ideas' (local forms the myth takes). The Hero with a Thousand Faces focused on commonality; The Masks of God emphasized historical and cultural variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying mythic templates, preserve universal emotional/structural motifs while adapting surface details, rituals, and symbols to fit specific cultures or settings. Avoid flattening cultural specificity in favor of a generic universalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero's journey as transformative arc (suffering, encounter, return)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hero's Journey was the story of the man or woman who, through great suffering, reached an experience of the eternal source and returned with gifts powerful enough to set their society free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the protagonist undergoes genuine trials, an encounter with a transformative source (psychic/spiritual insight or skill), and a meaningful return that impacts the world. The 'boon' should be tangible or symbolic and alter social relations or the hero's self-understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the artist/creative mythology in modernity
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell believed that in the modern world the function served by formal, traditional mythological systems has been taken on by individual creators such as artists and philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a writer, consciously act as a modern mythmaker: craft works that supply ritual, meaning, or psychological guidance for contemporary readers rather than merely rehashing ancient forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical adaptation for media and writing (story circle, memos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell's ideas have been adapted for practical storytelling (e.g., Christopher Vogler's 'A Practical Guide to The Hero With a Thousand Faces', Dan Harmon's story circle) and used by filmmakers and novelists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adapted, stage-based tools (Vogler's memo, Harmon's circle, three-act/beat templates) to translate Campbellian stages into workable plotting beats for screenplays, novels, and games. Treat these adaptations as tools, not orthodoxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interpreting myth as history/biography/science
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the poetry of myth is interpreted as biography, history, or science, it is killed; myths are living images and lose power when reduced to remote facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep mythic language evocative and symbolic; resist literalizing or historicizing symbolic elements in ways that strip them of mystery. Use ambiguous or polyvalent imagery to retain vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ritual and enactment to convey mythic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols and mythic metaphors point to transcendent reality, and their enactment through ritual can give the participant a sense of that ultimate mystery as an experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enacted rituals, repeated symbolic actions, or liturgical scenes to make mythic meanings experiential for characters and readers; rituals can dramatize internal transformation externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selection bias and overgeneralization (critique of monomyth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics say Campbell could 'construct a monomyth of the hero only by citing those stories that fit his preconceived mold, and leaving out equally valid stories… which did not fit the pattern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking universal patterns, test the model against counterexamples and alternative traditions. Do not cherry-pick stories to fit a theory; document sources and acknowledge variance to avoid reductive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly accuracy and humility (limits of expertise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell's Sanskrit scholarship and some historical claims were questioned; critics accused him of superficial knowledge in areas requiring specialist competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground mythic claims in careful research or collaboration with specialists for culturally specific material. Acknowledge epistemic limits and avoid asserting linguistic or historical expertise you do not possess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of oversimplification and interpretive flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell has been criticised for oversimplification of historical matters and a tendency to make myth mean whatever he wanted it to mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain rigor in interpretation: separate evidence from metaphorical reading, and avoid retrofitting diverse narratives into a single forced meaning. Use plurality of readings rather than monolithic assertions.
